overview: This bill changes how the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) helps communities prepare for disasters before they strike. It defines the "latest published editions" of building codes, which FEMA's disaster-prevention grants encourage communities to adopt, as the two most recent editions rather than only the newest one. It also creates a pilot program, running until September 30, 2030, that lets states and local governments use up to 10 percent of FEMA's yearly pre-disaster mitigation grant money to give homeowners grants to make their houses sturdier, such as by raising homes above flood levels, adding tornado safe rooms, retrofitting for earthquakes or wildfires, or strengthening roofs against wind. Grants under the pilot must go to people who show financial need, and FEMA must report on the results. The bill also removes one paragraph from the rules for a FEMA revolving loan program for disaster-resilience projects. As of October 3, 2025, the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee had approved it and it was placed on the House calendar.
for: Supporters say helping lower-income homeowners strengthen their houses before a disaster is cheaper than rebuilding afterward, and accepting the two most recent building code editions gives communities more realistic flexibility.
against: Critics say counting older code editions as current could slow the adoption of the newest safety standards, and setting aside part of a limited grant pot for individual homes could leave less money for larger community-wide projects.
